title: 1985 AHSME Problem 27
statement: Consider a sequence \(x_1,\) \(x_2,\) \(x_3,\) \(\ldots,\) defined by \[ \begin{aligned} x_1&=\sqrt[3]{3},\\ x_2&=(\sqrt[3]{3})^{\sqrt[3]{3}}. \end{aligned} \] and in general \[ x_n=(x_{n-1})^{\sqrt[3]{3}} \] for \(n\gt1.\) What is the smallest value of \(n\) for which \(x_n\) is an integer?

solutions.text:
Let \(c=\sqrt[3]{3}.\) Repeated application of the recurrence gives \[ x_n=3^{\frac{c^{\,n-1}}{3}}, \] so \(x_4=3^{\frac{c^3}{3}}=3.\) It remains to rule out the first three terms. The sequence is strictly increasing. Also \(c\lt\frac{3}{2},\) so \[ x_2=c^c \lt\left(\frac32\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \lt2. \] Finally \(x_3=3^{\frac{1}{c}}.\) Since \(2^c\lt2^{\frac{3}{2}}\lt3,\) we have \(x_3\gt2,\) while \(\frac{1}{c}\lt1\) gives \(x_3\lt3.\) Thus \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) are not integers, and the first integral term is \(x_4.\)

Therefore the correct answer is C.
hints: Let \(c=\sqrt[3]{3}\) and track the exponent of \(3\)
Show that \(x_n=3^{\frac{c^{\,n-1}}{3}}\) and examine the first four terms
